15.bp: Online shoppers face an explosion of choice—millions of products across countless websites. The real problem is cognitive overload: humans cannot realistically evaluate all options, read all reviews, and compare prices across the web. Agentic systems (AI agents that act autonomously) promise to do this tedious exploration work for us, automatically curating the best matches to what we actually want.
15.wh: Testing whether an AI agent can truly help a shopper is harder than it looks. Existing benchmarks (standardized tests) focus on toy scenarios: a single website, a straightforward lookup, no real personalization. They don't measure whether an agent can handle the sprawling, contradictory mess of the real web—nor whether it can learn that you, specifically, want lightweight hiking boots under $120, not the most reviewed option.
15.ap: AgenticShop creates a realistic test suite with three key pieces: (1) real shopping scenarios that require cross-website exploration, not just lookups; (2) diverse user profiles with specific, conflicting preferences (budget, style, features); and (3) a checklist-based evaluation—does the agent's final product list actually match what a person said they wanted?
15.ww: Personalization matters because different shoppers have fundamentally different goals. An agent that finds the 'best' product for everyone is useless—it must learn to distinguish between someone hunting for deals and someone willing to overpay for premium quality. By embedding real preferences into the test, you can see whether agents actually adapt.
15.po: The paper shows that today's agents fall short: they struggle to curate personalized results in open-web settings. This matters because it reveals a concrete gap—agents are not yet ready as personal shopping assistants, and researchers now have a principled way to measure progress.

16.bp: Many datasets in the real world can be viewed as networks of relationships: social links, biological interactions, or website links. When these relationships come in different types (labeled edges—say, 'friend' vs 'colleague'), you want to group nodes so that similar nodes cluster together *and* their connection types match up. Think of it as: if two people belong to the same social circle, most of their shared links should be of the same type.
16.wh: The naive approach would be to ignore the labels and just cluster based on network structure, or to treat each label separately—but that loses information. The real challenge: you want to assign a color (group) to each node such that when two nodes connect, their colors should match the color of the edge between them. This is mathematically hard (NP-hard), meaning no known algorithm solves it perfectly in reasonable time.
16.ap: This paper offers the first combinatorial approximation algorithm—a method that finds a solution *guaranteed* to be better than two times worse than the true optimal, using only discrete graph-manipulation operations (no floating-point math). Prior approaches achieved at best a 2× approximation factor (twice as bad as optimal); this one breaks that barrier.
16.ww: Combinatorial algorithms scale better on large networks because they avoid costly linear-algebra operations. By working directly with graph structure, you can handle massive, real-world networks that would choke a more sophisticated approach. A tighter approximation bound means the algorithm gives you fewer false clusters.
16.po: Researchers now have a faster, more precise tool for clustering typed networks—useful for organizing heterogeneous web data without sacrificing optimality guarantees. This matters in practice for systems that must cluster millions of user-generated relationships in real time.

17.bp: Knowledge graphs (databases of facts like 'Einstein was a physicist') are the backbone of search engines, fact-checking, and AI systems. But the real world is conditional: 'Einstein was a physicist' becomes richer when you add 'except during his diplomatic years.' These conditional qualifiers—the who, where, when, under what circumstances—are crucial for capturing nuanced truth.
17.wh: Existing information extraction (automatically pulling facts from text) methods treat facts and conditions as flat structures with no hierarchy. They also consider every possible way to combine a fact with a condition—a massive search space that wastes compute and introduces errors. The real obstacle: how do you represent the *structure* of a fact-plus-conditions (a quintuple) in a way that an AI can reason about?
17.ap: Diff-CIE uses a star graph—a structure where one central fact triple sits in the middle and conditions radiate outward like leaves. Then it treats extraction as a 'denoising' process: start with noisy nodes (messy candidate facts and conditions) and progressively refine them into clean quintuples. This reduces the explosive search space from 'all combinations' to a fixed, finite set.
17.ww: Explicit structure matters because it mirrors how humans think about conditions: a fact is primary, and conditions modify it. By anchoring conditions to facts (not treating them as floating independent items), the algorithm can use learned constraints to stabilize the extraction. The deterministic matching strategy acts like a guardrail, preventing wild, meaningless refinements.
17.po: The method extracts more accurate conditional knowledge triples—useful for building semantic webs that understand nuance and context. This unlocks richer representations for fact-checking, search, and knowledge AI.

18.bp: Amazon and Apple sell their own products on their platforms, competing directly with third-party sellers. This seems like a conflict of interest—shouldn't platforms be neutral? The real economic question is: when does a platform rationally choose to enter a product category, and how does that choice affect seller innovation? Understanding this shapes policy around platform fairness.
18.wh: The tension is strategic: if you're a seller, how do you innovate and decide what products to launch when you know the platform owner might copy your success and use its preferential position to outcompete you? If you're the platform, when should you enter—immediately, or only after a seller proves there's real demand? Standard game theory (assuming one rational party) fails here because you have multiple strategic players simultaneously learning from each other's moves.
18.ap: The paper frames this as a Stackelberg game—the platform commits to an entry policy first (e.g., 'I enter if a product gets more than X sales'), then sellers decide what to launch knowing this policy. With one seller, they use a Gittins-index policy (a mathematically optimal way to balance trying new products versus exploiting known winners). With multiple sellers, they use deep reinforcement learning to simulate what sellers would do in competition.
18.ww: The Stackelberg model works because it captures real causality: the platform, being powerful, moves first and credibly constrains its own future actions ('I won't enter this category'). Sellers then rationally respond. This structure explains why empirical markets like Amazon and Google Play show measurable patterns of platform entry following seller success.
18.po: The paper reveals the incentives driving platform entry decisions and seller innovation strategies, with direct implications for regulation. It shows quantitatively how platform entry policies can either encourage or suppress third-party innovation—actionable insight for protecting market diversity.

19.bp: Machine-learning models trained on historical data often inherit and amplify human biases. If a hiring model is trained on past hiring decisions that favored men, it will likely recommend men in the future. Fairness in machine learning means ensuring predictions don't discriminate unfairly. The question this paper asks: if you pre-train a model on synthetic data generated using causal reasoning, does that help with fairness?
19.wh: Foundation models for tabular (spreadsheet-like) data show impressive accuracy but fairness remains a black box. TabPFN, a popular tabular foundation model, is pre-trained on thousands of synthetic datasets designed using causal reasoning—the idea is that by understanding causal relationships (not just correlations), the model should make fairer predictions. But does it actually?
19.ap: The paper systematically tests TabPFN's fairness on real-world prediction tasks under different kinds of data shift—scenarios where the test data differs from training data in systematic ways (e.g., missing values that are not random). They measure both fairness (do predictions treat protected groups equally?) and accuracy, across multiple model sizes and datasets.
19.ww: Causal pre-training helps because causal models are designed to ignore spurious correlations—connections that are accidental, not mechanically real. For example, if the training data happens to show that tall people earn more, a causal model might ignore height if it's not mechanistically tied to income. This should reduce unfair bias.
19.po: The results are mixed: TabPFN does improve fairness over baselines, but the gains are modest and inconsistent, especially when data is missing in biased ways. This tells practitioners that causal pre-training is not a panacea—fairness requires additional interventions, even with theoretically principled pre-training.

20.bp: Large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT generate text one word at a time by computing a probability for each possible next word. But there's a puzzle: does the model's probability distribution over words match what the real task needs? If the task is book recommendation, should the model output diverse suggestions or stick to safe, popular picks? The paper uncovers two fundamentally different LLM types that answer this differently.
20.wh: Models vary unpredictably in their sampling behavior. Some models change their probability distribution drastically from one token to the next (high variability), while others are more stable. But which is better? And for what tasks? The problem is that no one has systematically measured whether a model's probability distribution actually aligns with what a task requires.
20.ap: The paper simulates controlled scenarios where they know the 'true' probability distribution a task needs, then measure how well each LLM's output distribution matches it. They identify two types: D-models (high step-to-step variability, poor alignment) and E-models (stable probabilities, good alignment). Then they test these two types on real tasks like code generation and product recommendation.
20.ww: Different tasks have different probability needs. Code generation might need stable, focused distributions (you don't want random variables named 'x' and 'xyzzy' equally often). Recommendations might need diversity (you want to occasionally suggest unexpected items, not just the most-sold product). By decomposing models into D and E types, you can make principled choices.
20.po: Practitioners can now match model type to task. If you need stable, predictable outputs, use an E-model; if you need diverse, exploratory outputs, use a D-model. This removes guesswork from LLM deployment in recommendation, search, and code-generation applications.

21.bp: Social media spreads false claims constantly. Fact-checking—verifying whether a claim is true—is essential for fighting misinformation, but manual fact-checking cannot scale. Automated fact-checking attempts to retrieve relevant evidence from the web and then decide whether a claim is supported by that evidence. The challenge is handling noise: not all retrieved facts are equally useful, and reasoning systems hallucinate (invent facts).
21.wh: Real-world fact-checking breaks in two places: (1) retrieved evidence is noisy—systems grab irrelevant or contradictory documents that mislead the verifier; and (2) verification models confidently assert things not actually supported by evidence. You need both clean evidence *and* careful reasoning to avoid false verdicts.
21.ap: SLED has two stages. First, it retrieves candidate evidence, then uses a pre-trained verifier to score each piece for credibility and relevance, filtering out noise. Second, it prompts an LLM to argue both for and against the claim (dual-perspective reasoning), simulates a debate between these arguments, then distills the outcome into a lightweight model for speed.
21.ww: Self-supervised denoising works because you can learn to spot noisy evidence without manual labels—the verifier sees which evidence actually helps downstream prediction. Multi-agent debate surfaces contradictions and forces the model to confront weak reasoning. Distillation into a small model keeps inference fast for web-scale deployment.
21.po: The method achieves state-of-the-art fact-checking on complex benchmarks by combining filtering (fewer false positives) with robust reasoning (avoiding hallucination). This matters because it makes automated fact-checking reliable enough to deploy against high-stakes misinformation.

22.bp: Social networks and the web generate continuous streams of events—user posts, purchases, clicks. Predicting future events (will this user click that article?) requires modeling how past events influence each other and how that influence changes over time. The real-world constraint: billions of events per day demand fast predictions, not slow, accurate ones.
22.wh: Existing neural methods struggle with two contradictory demands. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are sequential but can't 'see' far into the past—early events fade from memory. Graph neural networks (GNNs) handle relationships well but become prohibitively slow on large, real-time event streams. Neither scales to web-scale prediction.
22.ap: Fourier Graph Learning shifts perspective: instead of thinking about events in time order (the time domain), think about them in terms of oscillating patterns (the frequency domain). Each node and edge becomes a complex number—the real part encodes what the event is about, the imaginary part encodes its temporal rhythm. Multiplying complex numbers in frequency space is faster than sequential processing.
22.ww: Frequency-domain reasoning captures both short-term bursts and long-term trends efficiently. A semantic-aware frequency filter can emphasize long-term dependencies you care about while dampening noise. This is faster than running a GNN because matrix multiplication in frequency space scales better than message passing on large graphs.
22.po: Fourier Graph Neural Networks dramatically reduce compute cost while maintaining accuracy. For large-scale event prediction on platforms like Twitter or e-commerce sites, this means you can predict faster and adapt to new user behavior in real time.

23.bp: E-commerce platforms care about conversion rate (does a click turn into a purchase?) but also refund rate (does the purchase get returned?). Net conversion rate combines both: it measures whether a customer actually keeps a purchase. This matters because a high-conversion, high-refund rate looks good on paper but represents unhappy customers and lost money.
23.wh: Net conversion rate prediction is harder than conversion-rate prediction because of cascaded delays: there's a delay from click to purchase, then another (often longer) delay from purchase to refund decision. And the two delays interact—what predicts 'will buy?' is different from 'will keep?'. Existing methods, designed for single-stage prediction, don't handle this multi-stage cascade.
23.ap: The paper introduces CASCADE, a large real-world dataset from Taobao with millions of records showing clicks, conversions, refunds, and delays. They analyze it and find three key patterns: (1) net conversion shows temporal trends; (2) modeling conversion and refund separately, then combining, beats directly modeling net conversion; and (3) delay time itself is predictive—faster conversions have different refund patterns than slow ones. They then propose TESLA, a method that continuously learns these patterns.
23.wh: Cascaded delay modeling works because the two stages have different causal mechanisms. A product that converts quickly might refund quickly too (impulse buy + regret). A product that converts slowly might be carefully considered (lower refund). By modeling both mechanisms, you capture these dynamics.
23.po: TESLA provides a more accurate picture of true customer satisfaction on e-commerce platforms. This enables better product ranking, better inventory decisions, and better business metrics that actually reflect real user value, not just transaction velocity.

24.bp: Federated learning lets a machine-learning model learn from data spread across millions of users' phones without sending raw data to a central server—each phone trains locally, then shares only the learned weights. But users have different preferences and data, so a one-size-fits-all global model performs poorly. Personalized federated learning tries to adapt the global model to each user's specific data.
24.wh: Sharing the feature extractor (the network's early layers that learn general patterns) seems like the right compromise between global and local. But this assumption has never been rigorously tested. The real tension: if the global feature extractor is misaligned with what individual users need, forcing everyone to use it degrades personalization.
24.ap: pFedDKS proposes a principled split: use neural collapse theory (a mathematical framework showing how deep neural networks organize learned representations) to prove that the feature extractor should be partially, not fully, shared. It detaches global features and local features by learning separate 'prototypes' (exemplar representations) for shared vs. personalized layers.
24.wh: Neural collapse shows that well-trained networks organize representations in a specific geometric pattern. By forcing shared and local features to respect this structure, the model can maintain global knowledge while preserving user-specific characteristics. This is more stable than arbitrary layer-wise sharing.
24.po: pFedDKS outperforms prior federated-learning methods, enabling personalization without sacrificing privacy or forcing users to contribute to unrelated global models. For platforms like health apps and keyboards, this means better accuracy while respecting user privacy.

25.bp: Recommendation systems increasingly use large language models to generate explanations for why an item was recommended ('We think you'll like this coat because you liked the blue winter jacket last month'). These explanations build trust. But in the real world, user interaction histories are messy: accidental clicks, forgotten purchases, data errors. If the explanation changes wildly when one click is removed, users won't trust it.
25.wh: No one has systematically measured whether LLM-generated explanations are robust—whether they stay consistent despite realistic noise in user data. This matters because a brittle explanation system could amplify noise into unstable, contradictory recommendations.
25.ap: RobustExplain creates five types of realistic user-data perturbations (accidental clicks, missing values, temporal shifts, etc.) and tests them at multiple severity levels against four large LLMs (7 billion to 70 billion parameters). It measures robustness across four dimensions: whether key ideas survive (semantic), whether keywords stay (keyword), whether the explanation structure holds (structural), and whether length is stable.
25.ww: Multiple dimensions of robustness matter because explanations serve multiple purposes. Semantic stability means the core reasoning doesn't flip. Keyword stability means the recommendation itself doesn't change. Structural stability means the explanation remains readable. By measuring all four, you get a complete picture.
25.po: Current LLM explanations show only moderate robustness—larger models help but not by much. This establishes a concrete benchmark and shows that recommendation explanations need additional safeguards (denoising, consistency checks) to be trustworthy in real-world noisy data.

26.bp: Large language models use a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture—instead of one monolithic network, you have dozens of specialized sub-networks (experts) and a router that decides which experts to use for each input. This is efficient: you don't activate all experts every time. But routing is stateless and wasteful: if two similar inputs arrive, the router re-explores which experts to use, wasting compute.
26.wh: Stateless routing means every input requires full routing computation, even if similar inputs were just routed. On web-scale systems handling millions of requests per second (search, dialogue), this repeated exploration wastes billions of operations. Additionally, routing is unstable: the same input at different times might be routed differently, creating inconsistent behavior.
26.ap: RMS-MoE adds memory: a Co-Activation Memory stores which expert teams worked well for which semantic patterns. For new input, it retrieves similar past patterns' expert assignments, uses those as a prior, then combines that prior with live routing decisions via a learnable gate. This is more efficient (retrieve + fuse rather than full routing) and more stable (similar inputs get similar expert assignments).
26.wh: Retrieval-augmented routing works because input patterns tend to repeat—the same search query or dialogue turn appears many times. By caching expert team assignments for semantic patterns, you can amortize the routing cost. The learnable gate ensures the retrieved prior can be updated if live routing signals something different.
26.po: RMS-MoE achieves a 26% latency reduction, 2.7-point accuracy gain, and 3.3% better routing stability on web-scale tasks. This translates to faster search and dialogue systems that behave more predictably—directly valuable for deployed LLM applications.

27.bp: E-commerce recommendations operate at the item level (show 'blue winter jacket'), but users actually purchase at a finer granularity—specific variants (size M, color navy, material wool). Price varies by variant: the jacket might be $60 in polyester or $150 in wool. This granularity mismatch means you lose critical information about what users actually want and how they value price.
27.wh: Moving to variant-level prediction seems obvious but is impractical: millions of items times dozens of variants each creates a sparse prediction problem (most variants have zero historical purchases), plus inference becomes prohibitively expensive. You need to compress the space without losing price signals.
27.ap: PSKU4Rec groups variants by price (Price SKU)—variants of the same item at similar prices are treated as one unit. This reduces sparsity by 6×. The model then learns intra-item price preferences (does this user prefer premium or budget variants?) and cross-item price patterns. At inference, it uses these to estimate the price-specific conversion rate and show the most appropriate product image for each user.
27.wh: Grouping by price works because price is the main variant dimension users care about. Two $50 variants (different materials but same price) are interchangeable for most users; two variants of the same item at $30 vs $80 are fundamentally different purchase decisions. By collapsing on price, you retain signal while compressing sparse space.
27.po: PSKU4Rec improves both conversion prediction and price consistency on Taobao's real data. This enables better product ranking, more honest pricing (exposure price matches transaction price), and higher user satisfaction because recommendations match actual purchasing patterns.

28.bp: Data marketplaces—platforms where data owners sell data to consumers (e.g., 'I'll sell you my anonymized customer purchase history')—require privacy: data owners don't want buyers to see raw data. Differential privacy (a mathematical guarantee) adds noise to data so that individual records can't be reverse-engineered. But who adds the noise? If a central marketplace adds it, sellers must trust the marketplace. If a seller adds it, buyers trust no one.
28.wh: Existing differential-privacy schemes for data trading require trusting either the seller or a central authority. Sellers can't prove they added exactly the right noise; marketplaces can't be trusted not to peek at raw data. Additionally, malicious attackers might corrupt the noise injection process. You need a decentralized, trustworthy mechanism.
28.ap: Xemis uses multi-party computation (MPC)—a cryptographic technique where multiple parties jointly compute a result without any single party seeing intermediate values. Specifically, it uses a 'distributed noise sharing' protocol (b-DNS) where multiple parties collaboratively generate noise shares such that when combined, they produce exactly the right privacy-preserving noise. No single party controls the noise.
28.wh: MPC works because the noise is generated by consensus: if even one party is honest, the noise is trustworthy. Byzantine robustness means the scheme survives even if some parties try to cheat. The batched bits-expansion mechanism reduces the cryptographic overhead dramatically (12.7× faster than prior methods).
28.po: Xemis enables decentralized, trustworthy data trading without requiring faith in a single marketplace or seller. Sellers can prove they're not leaking data; buyers can trust the privacy level; attackers can't corrupt the noise. This unlocks real data markets where neither party has total control.

29.bp: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) uses a large language model to answer questions by first retrieving relevant documents from the web, then reasoning over those documents. The quality of the answer depends on retrieving good documents. But what makes a document 'good' isn't always obvious: relevance to the question, credibility, and usefulness all matter differently depending on the question.
29.wh: Current RAG systems assume retrieved documents are relevant and treat them equally in answer generation. But retrieved documents vary wildly in quality. A document might be topically related (technically relevant) but poorly written, outdated, or misleading. How can the language model tell which retrieved documents to trust and emphasize?
29.ap: OpenDecoder explicitly scores retrieved documents along three dimensions: relevance (topical match to the question), ranking score (where the document appeared in search results), and query performance prediction (a meta-measure of how useful the document is likely to be for this specific question). These scores become features that the LLM's generation process can see and use.
29.wh: Explicit quality signals help the model make calibrated use of noisy context. Rather than blindly incorporating whatever is retrieved, the model can learn to ignore low-quality documents and emphasize high-quality ones. This is more robust than hoping the LLM's internal reasoning automatically filters.
29.po: OpenDecoder outperforms standard RAG on five benchmark datasets, especially when context is noisy. This matters for deployed question-answering systems where retrieval is imperfect and robustness to low-quality documents is critical.
